posts.title: Books That Keep My Creativity Sharp
posts.excerpt: The books I come back to when the ideas stop flowing — on beating creative block, generating ideas, and learning to see like an artist.
posts.body:
A running list of the books I come back to when the ideas stop flowing, the work feels stuck, or I just need a reminder of why I make things. Split into how I actually use them.

### When you're blocked or scared of the work

![The War of Art](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781936891023-M.jpg)
**The War of Art** — *Steven Pressfield*. The best short book on “Resistance” — that voice that finds any excuse not to start. I re-read it before big projects.

![Art & Fear](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780961454739-M.jpg)
**Art & Fear** — *David Bayles & Ted Orland*. Written *by* artists, *for* artists, about the real reasons people quit making art. If you buy one book on this list, this one.

![Big Magic](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781594634710-M.jpg)
**Big Magic** — *Elizabeth Gilbert*. On making creative work without demanding it pay the rent or validate your ego. Freeing.

![The Artist's Way](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780874776940-M.jpg)
**The Artist's Way** — *Julia Cameron*. Famous for “morning pages.” A bit woo for some, but the unblocking exercises work.

### On ideas and process

![Steal Like an Artist](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780761169253-M.jpg)
**Steal Like an Artist** — *Austin Kleon*. Nothing is original; everything is remix. Short, punchy, endlessly quotable. Pair it with *Show Your Work!* and *Keep Going*.

![The Creative Act: A Way of Being](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780593652886-M.jpg)
**The Creative Act: A Way of Being** — *Rick Rubin*. Less “how-to,” more a way of paying attention to the world as source material.

![Where Good Ideas Come From](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781594485381-M.jpg)
**Where Good Ideas Come From** — *Steven Johnson*. Where innovation actually happens — the “adjacent possible,” slow hunches, and the collision of ideas.

![Creativity: Flow and the Psychology of Discovery and Invention](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780060928209-M.jpg)
**Creativity: Flow and the Psychology of Discovery and Invention** — *Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi*. The research behind “flow,” the state every artist chases.

### Made for people who work in images

![Ways of Seeing](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780140135152-M.jpg)
**Ways of Seeing** — *John Berger*. Rewires how you look at images and why they carry the meaning they do.

![Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781585429202-M.jpg)
**Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain** — *Betty Edwards*. Half drawing skill, half a lesson in *perception* — seeing what's actually there instead of what you think is there.

### For creative careers and teams

![Creativity, Inc.](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780812993011-M.jpg)
**Creativity, Inc.** — *Ed Catmull*. Pixar's co-founder on protecting creativity inside a studio. Required reading if you work in games or film.

![The Practice](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780593328972-M.jpg)
**The Practice** — *Seth Godin*. Ship the work. Trust the process over the outcome.

*What's on your shelf? I'm always looking for the next one — hit me up on [ArtStation](https://www.artstation.com/mikicompany) or [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/mikicompany).*

posts.title: Office Mural
posts.excerpt: A 10×3 m mural for Offworld Industries' studio — designed and hand-painted in five days with latex paint, dabbers, aerosol, brushes, and a lot of coffee.
posts.body:
Last October, I was commissioned by **Offworld Industries** to design and paint a mural for the studio. The entire wall is approximately **10 × 3 m** — here are some photos and video from the process. \ :) /

![Office mural for Offworld Industries](https://cdna.artstation.com/p/media_assets/images/images/001/021/164/large/PA170613.jpg?1669496778)

I painted it over **five days**, using a mix of latex-based paint, paint dabbers, some aerosol, and good old paintbrushes — together with a lot of coffee.

Thank you to everyone who contributed to the wall. You guys are the best <3

posts.title: Breaking Into Games as an Environment Artist
posts.excerpt: The question I get asked most — how to land your first environment-art job in games, from someone who reviews portfolios for a living.
posts.body:
I get this question a lot — in DMs, from students, from friends of friends trying to switch careers. "How do I actually get a job making environments for games?" Here's my honest answer, from the other side of the hiring table.

## Your portfolio is the whole ballgame
Not your degree, not your software list, not your cover letter. When I look at a candidate, I open the portfolio first and everything else second. So put your energy there.

**Four to six finished, focused pieces beat twenty half-finished ones.** A short portfolio of strong environment work says "I have taste and I finish things." A giant pile of props and unfinished scenes says the opposite.

## Show environments, not just assets
A lot of aspiring environment artists show a folder of individual props and materials. That's fine to *have*, but the job is building **spaces** — so show spaces. A believable corner of a world, well-lit, with a clear sense of place and story, is worth more than ten hero props on turntables.

## Pick a lane and make the portfolio scream it
"Environment artist" is broad. Are you a **prop/material** artist, a **modular/kit** builder, a **level artist** composing spaces, or a **world/set-dresser**? You don't have to marry one forever, but a portfolio that clearly points at a role is far easier to hire than a generalist blur.

## Fundamentals still win
Software changes every couple of years; **composition, value, lighting, scale, and storytelling** don't. The portfolios that stop me are almost never the most technically dense — they're the ones where someone clearly understands how to lead the eye and make a space *feel* like something.

A handful of books that actually teach this — worth more than any single tutorial:

![How to Draw](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781933492735-M.jpg)

**How to Draw** — *Scott Robertson & Thomas Bertling*. Perspective and structural drawing; the backbone of building believable spaces.

![How to Render](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781933492964-M.jpg)

**How to Render** — *Scott Robertson*. Light, shadow, and materials — the companion to *How to Draw*.

![Color and Light](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780740797712-M.jpg)

**Color and Light** — *James Gurney*. The reference for making light read convincingly.

![Light for Visual Artists](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781856697095-M.jpg)

**Light for Visual Artists** — *Richard Yot*. Practical lighting theory that translates straight to 3D.

![Framed Ink](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781933492957-M.jpg)

**Framed Ink** — *Marcos Mateu-Mestre*. Composition and visual storytelling — how to lead the eye through a scene.

![Imaginative Realism](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780740785504-M.jpg)

**Imaginative Realism** — *James Gurney*. Making imagined worlds feel real.

![Architecture: Form, Space, and Order](https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9781118745083-M.jpg)

**Architecture: Form, Space, and Order** — *Francis D.K. Ching*. How built space actually works — gold for environment artists.

## Learn the pipeline, not just the buttons
Knowing ZBrush and Substance isn't the same as knowing how to build for a game. Learn **modular construction, trim sheets, texel density, and working in-engine** (Unreal is a safe bet). Show at least one piece built and lit *in engine*, not just a Marmoset render — it tells me you can actually ship.

## Recreate, then create
A great way to learn the bar: **recreate a small environment from a game you admire.** It teaches you the standard and gives you something recognizable to show. Then do original work that proves you can design, not just copy.

## Presentation is part of the craft
Beauty shots, a clean lighting pass, a short breakdown of your process, and a tidy ArtStation. If two portfolios have equal work, the one that's *presented* well wins. Showing your process also signals that you're teachable and organized — things leads care about a lot.

## Be coachable, and get real feedback
Post in art Discords, get portfolio reviews, find a mentor. Then — and this is the part people skip — **actually act on the feedback.** Being easy to give notes to is a genuine hiring signal. Nobody wants to work with someone who argues with every critique.

## Network without being weird
You don't need to "sell" yourself. Just be part of the community: share your work, cheer on other artists, help beginners. Most of my opportunities came from people I'd simply been around and been decent to.

## On actually applying
- **Apply before you feel ready.** You never will. If your work is close, send it.
- **Tailor lightly.** A studio that makes stylized worlds wants to see you *can* do stylized.
- **Side doors are real doors.** Outsourcing studios, QA, and junior/associate roles all lead inward. Don't wait for the perfect title.
- **Rejection is the baseline, not a verdict.** I got plenty. Keep making work; the portfolio you have in six months is the one that lands the job.

## The short version
Make a small, sharp portfolio of *environments*, nail the fundamentals, show one thing built in-engine, present it well, be someone people want to work with, and apply relentlessly. That's most of it.

*Got a portfolio you want a gut-check on? I'm around on [ArtStation](https://www.artstation.com/mikicompany) and [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/mikicompany).*

posts.title: A Practical Guide to Sculpting in Blender
posts.excerpt: How sculpting in Blender really works — the topology systems, the brushes that matter, a big-to-small workflow, and how to take a sculpt all the way to a game-ready asset. With sources.
posts.body:
Blender's sculpting tools have quietly become some of the best in the industry — and they're free. I use them constantly for props, rocks, hero assets and anything organic that needs to feel hand-made before it becomes a clean game model. This is the guide I wish I'd had when I started: how sculpting in Blender actually works, the tools that matter, and how to take a sculpt all the way to a game-ready asset.

If you don't have Blender yet, grab it from [blender.org/download](https://www.blender.org/download/) — and keep the official [Blender Manual: Sculpting](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/sculpt_paint/sculpting/index.html) open in a tab. It's genuinely good documentation.

## What sculpting actually is

Sculpting treats your mesh like a lump of digital clay. Instead of pushing individual vertices around, you drag brushes across the surface and the underlying geometry deforms — building forms up, carving them in, smoothing them out. To make that feel like clay, you need **a lot** of polygons, which is where Blender's three topology systems come in (more on those below).

The single most important setup tip: **use a pen tablet.** Pressure sensitivity drives brush size and strength, and sculpting with a mouse is like painting with a brick. A basic Wacom or an XP-Pen is plenty to start.

## The topology decision: Dyntopo vs. Multires vs. Voxel Remesh

This trips up every beginner, so let's be clear. Sculpting needs density, and there are three ways to get it:

- **Dynamic Topology (Dyntopo)** adds and removes detail *as you draw*, subdividing the mesh only where the brush touches. Great for fast, exploratory blockouts and when you don't know the final shape yet. Downside: messy, triangulated topology.
- **Voxel Remesh** rebuilds your whole mesh into an even grid of polygons at a resolution you choose (`Ctrl+R` in Sculpt Mode). This is my go-to for blocking organic forms — sculpt roughly, remesh to add uniform density, sculpt more, repeat. Clean, even, no stretching.
- **Multiresolution (Multires) modifier** keeps a clean base mesh and stores your sculpted detail on subdivision *levels*, so you can drop to a low level to change big forms and jump up to add fine detail. This is the classic film/character pipeline and the one that plays nicest with baking later. See the [Multiresolution modifier docs](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/modeling/modifiers/generate/multiresolution.html).

A practical rule: **Voxel Remesh to find the form, Multires to detail it, Dyntopo when you're just playing.**

## The brushes that actually matter

Blender ships with a big brush list, but you'll live in about eight of them. Hold `F` to scale brush size and `Shift+F` for strength — do that thousands of times and it becomes muscle memory.

- **Draw** — the basic "add clay" brush. Your default.
- **Clay Strips** — the workhorse. Builds up volume in confident, flat-edged strokes. Most of my blocking is Clay Strips.
- **Grab** (`G`) — grabs and moves a whole region. For big gestural changes to the silhouette.
- **Smooth** (hold `Shift` with any brush) — averages the surface. You'll use this more than any single brush; sculpting is a constant dance between adding form and smoothing it.
- **Crease** — pinches a sharp valley. For seams, folds, and where two forms meet.
- **Pinch** — pulls surface together to tighten an edge.
- **Inflate** — pushes the surface out along its normals; good for puffing up soft forms.
- **Flatten / Scrape** — planes off high spots. Essential for hard-surface-ish and rock work.
- **Snake Hook** — pulls out tentacles, horns, branches from the surface.

The full reference lives in the manual under [Sculpt Tools](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/sculpt_paint/sculpting/index.html). Don't try to memorize all of them — learn the eight above cold first.

## Masking, Face Sets and the Pose brush

These are what separate a beginner sculpt from a controlled one:

- **Masking** (`M` to paint a mask, `Ctrl+I` to invert) protects areas from your brush so you can work one region without wrecking its neighbour.
- **Face Sets** group the surface into logical chunks you can isolate, hide, or grow a mask from — invaluable for keeping a complex sculpt organized.
- **Pose, Cloth and Boundary brushes** deform larger areas naturally — the Pose brush rotates a limb from a virtual joint, the Cloth brush simulates fabric folds in real time. They feel like magic the first time.

## A workflow that works

Whatever you're sculpting, the order is always **big → medium → small**:

1. **Blockout.** Start from a simple base (a sphere, a cube, or a fast Dyntopo blob) and nail the **silhouette and proportions** with Grab and Clay Strips. Squint at it. If the silhouette doesn't read now, no amount of detail will save it.
2. **Establish forms.** Voxel Remesh to add density, then define the primary and secondary masses — the big anatomical or structural shapes. Keep smoothing.
3. **Refine.** Add Multires levels and work in the medium forms — muscle groups, rock planes, wood grain direction, wrinkles.
4. **Detail.** Only now do you add fine surface detail: pores, cracks, scratches, fabric weave. This is where alpha brushes come in.

The mistake everyone makes is jumping to step 4 too early. Detail on top of weak forms just looks noisy.

## Detailing with alphas and textures

Fine detail is faster to *stamp* than to sculpt by hand. Blender lets you plug a grayscale **alpha** (a height map) into a brush's texture slot and dab or drag it across the surface — instant scales, skin pores, stone pitting, cloth weave. You can paint your own, or grab high-quality sets from places like [Texturing.xyz](https://www.texturing.xyz/) for skin and [Poly Haven](https://polyhaven.com/) for free CC0 textures you can repurpose as alphas.

## From sculpt to game asset (the part people skip)

Here's where my day job comes in. A 4-million-triangle sculpt can't go into a game — you have to transfer its detail onto a lightweight model. The pipeline:

1. **Retopology** — build a clean, low-polygon mesh that follows your sculpt's forms. Blender has native retopo tools (snapping to surface with the Poly Build tool and Shrinkwrap), and the popular add-on [RetopoFlow](https://blendermarket.com/products/retopoflow) speeds it up a lot.
2. **UV unwrap** the low-poly so it has a flat texture layout.
3. **Bake** the high-poly detail down onto the low-poly as a **normal map** (and ambient occlusion, curvature, etc.). Blender bakes via Cycles — the [baking documentation](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/cycles/baking.html) covers the setup, and many artists bake in [Marmoset Toolbag](https://marmoset.co/toolbag/) or [Substance 3D Painter](https://www.adobe.com/products/substance3d/apps/painter.html) for speed and control.
4. **Texture** the low-poly using those baked maps as a base.

The result: the game engine renders a few thousand triangles that *look* like they have millions, because the lighting detail is faked in the normal map. That trick is the entire reason sculpting matters for games.

## Common beginner mistakes

- **Not enough (or way too much) geometry.** If the brush feels chunky, you need more density; if Blender is crawling, you have too much — remesh down or work on Multires.
- **Over-smoothing everything into mush.** Smooth deliberately, not reflexively.
- **Detailing before the forms are right.** Say it with me: silhouette first.
- **Never rotating the view.** Sculpt from every angle constantly — forms that look great from the front are often broken in profile.
- **Sculpting symmetrically forever.** Symmetry (`X` axis) is great for blocking, but turn it off and add asymmetry at the end so it doesn't look CG-perfect.

## Where to actually learn it

Reading only gets you so far — sculpting is a motor skill. These are the resources I recommend, all reputable:

- **[Blender Manual — Sculpting](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/sculpt_paint/sculpting/index.html)** — the official reference, surprisingly readable.
- **[Blender Studio](https://studio.blender.org/)** — the Blender org's own training and open-movie files.
- **[Grant Abbitt](https://www.youtube.com/@grabbitt)** — the best free beginner-friendly Blender sculpting teacher on YouTube.
- **[YanSculpts](https://www.youtube.com/@YanSculpts)** — focused specifically on sculpting, from a working character artist.
- **[FlippedNormals](https://flippednormals.com/)** — pro-level sculpting and pipeline courses (also great free YouTube content).
- **[CG Cookie](https://cgcookie.com/)** and **[ArtStation Learning](https://www.artstation.com/learning)** — structured, project-based courses.
- **[Blender Guru](https://www.youtube.com/@blenderguru)** — not sculpting-specific, but the best starting point for Blender fundamentals overall.

Pick one asset — a rock, a skull, a little creature — and sculpt it start to finish, retopo and bake included. You'll learn more from finishing one thing than from watching ten tutorials.

*Questions, or want me to break down a specific piece? Find me on [ArtStation](https://www.artstation.com/mikicompany) or [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/mikicompany).*
